ref: Eusebius, Church History 1.7.2–10 (Africanus, Letter to Aristides, quoted)
orig_url: not read (Greek of Eusebius HE 1.7 not yet located)
quote_en: But according to law he was the son of Eli, for Jacob, being the brother of the latter, raised up seed to him.
licence_note: English: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, NPNF2 vol. 1 (1890), public domain. Page read at newadvent.org; no explicit licence line seen on the page.
from_: But according to law he was the son
what_it_shows: Africanus (quoted by Eusebius) explains that the genealogies name Joseph as the son of Jacob 'by nature' and as the son of Eli 'according to law', because Jacob, the brother of the childless Eli, 'raised up seed' to him by the levirate custom. He says that Israel reckoned generations 'either according to nature or according to law', and that law applied 'whenever another raised up a child to the name of a brother dying childless'.
context: Eusebius quotes a letter of Julius Africanus to Aristides on the harmony of the two gospel genealogies, which Africanus gives 'which he had received from tradition' (Eusebius's words). Africanus rejects other harmonies as 'forced and deceptive' and proposes two levirate marriages to a single widow (Estha) by Matthan and Melchi. The purpose is apologetic: to show that both Matthew and Luke give true descent to Joseph.
limits: (1) The mechanism is levirate marriage (a dead man's name raised up through a brother), not adoption by a living father. Africanus does not say that adoption transmits lineage. (2) He calls Jacob's child Joseph 'his own son by nature', so the 'legal' sonship concerns Eli only, and only in the levirate case. (3) He states that the law of Moses did not allow marriage between tribes, so he treats Mary as of the same tribe (end of 1.7); this is about tribe through endogamy, not adoption. (4) It is a 3rd-century Christian reconstruction (date from general knowledge, not on the page), not a legal text, and Africanus himself says the account comes by tradition. (5) Eusebius (and Africanus) are reconciling the two genealogies; the text does not say that Joseph was legally Jesus' father, only that Joseph is reckoned as Eli's son 'according to law'. Read in context, the legal line runs to Eli, not to Jesus.
stance: commentator (Africanus, a Christian writer, quoted by Eusebius). Eusebius is reporting.

quote_orig: Ἰωσήφ, υἱὸς Δαβίδ, μὴ φοβηθῇς παραλαβεῖν Μαριὰμ τὴν γυναῖκά σου· τὸ γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν ἐκ Πνεύματός ἐστιν Ἁγίου.
quote_en: Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost.
licence_note: English: King James Version (1611), public domain (Project Gutenberg eBook #10). Greek: el.wikisource page footer states CC BY-SA 4.0 (share-alike; not in the brief's list of acceptable licences, so quote with attribution or check with team). Edition behind the Greek page is not named on the page.
from_: Joseph, thou son of David, fear not
to: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost.
what_it_shows: The angel addresses Joseph as 'son of David' (Matt 1:20) and tells him to take Mary as his wife, while the child is said to be conceived 'of the Holy Ghost'. In 1:21 the angel tells Joseph to call the child Jesus, and 1:25 says Joseph 'called his name Jesus' after the marriage. The text calls Joseph 'son of David' and names him as the one to name the child, but it never says that Joseph begets, adopts or legally fathers Jesus, and it never uses the word adoption.
context: Matthew's genealogy (1:1–17) ends at 1:16 with 'Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ'. 1:18–25 then narrates the angel's dream. The Greek 1:16 has the feminine relative 'ἐξ ἧς' (of whom), so the birth is tied to Mary, not to Joseph. Matthew's Greek in 1:18–25 is the basis for the Christian claim that Joseph's naming and taking of Mary gave the child a Davidic legal place.
limits: (1) Matthew 1:16 calls Joseph 'the husband of Mary' and says 'of whom' (Mary) Jesus was born; the text does not say Joseph is the father. (2) The address 'son of David' in 1:20 is to Joseph himself, which the source uses to identify Joseph as Davidic; it does not say the Davidic line passes to Jesus through him by law. (3) The naming in 1:21/1:25 is a command and an act; the text gives no legal theory (adoption, legal fatherhood or tribal transfer). (4) Matthew 1:18 says Mary was found with child 'of the Holy Ghost' before they came together; the virginal conception is explicit, which is the reason for the 'not by blood' claim, not evidence of legal adoption. (5) Luke 3:23 (below) calls Joseph 'as was supposed' the father, which some readers take as a limit on his sonship.

ref: Augustine, De consensu evangelistarum (Harmony of the Gospels) II.3.5
orig_url: not read (Latin of De consensu evangelistarum II.3.5 not yet located)
quote_en: Joseph may have had two fathers — namely, one by whom he was begotten, and a second by whom he may have been adopted. For it was an ancient custom also among that people to adopt children with the view of making sons for themselves of those whom they had not begotten.
licence_note: English: NPNF1 vol. 6 (Buffalo, 1888), ed. Philip Schaff, revised for New Advent by Kevin Knight; public domain. Page read at newadvent.org.
from_: Joseph may have had two fathers
to: those whom they had not begotten.
keys: by whom he may have been adopted
those whom they had not begotten
what_it_shows: Augustine says that Luke, in his genealogy, names as Joseph's father the man by whom Joseph was adopted, not the man who begot him, and that the line traced from David is the adopting father's line. He grounds this in the ancient custom of adopting children 'to make sons for themselves of those whom they had not begotten', citing Jacob's adoption of Ephraim and Manasseh.
context: Augustine (Book II of the Harmony of the Gospels) answers critics who ask why Matthew traces Joseph from David downward and Luke traces him upward to David. He offers the 'two fathers' solution: Matthew follows the begetting father (Jacob), Luke follows the adopting father (Heli). He then discusses Pharaoh's daughter adopting Moses and Jacob adopting Joseph's sons (Gen 48:5), and says that the twelve tribes arose from this adoption, with Levi omitted.
limits: (1) Augustine frames the two-father solution as a possibility answering critics: 'may have had two fathers', 'may have been adopted'. He does not say that Matthew or Luke says Joseph was adopted; he says Luke 'has named a father for Joseph' by adoption, which is his own inference. (2) He says the Lukan adoption makes 'Heli' the father in the line, but in II.3.6 he adds that even 'begotten' might be used 'in love' for an adopted son, which makes the adoption/begetting words loose. (3) Augustine's own phrase 'as both evangelists give a true narrative' is an apologetic premise. (4) He draws on the Old Testament adoption of Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen 48:5), but Gen 48:6 says Jacob's later-born children 'shall be called after the name of their brethren' (Rashi, see J-04, says they have no separate tribal name). (5) Augustine's text, as read, does not say that adoption transmits tribe to Jesus. (6) Augustine is a late 4th/early 5th-century writer (De consensu c. 400 AD), not an early source for legal practice; he is an exegete. (7) Other Fathers (Gregory of Nazianzus, Epiphanius, per a search snippet) hold that Luke gives Mary's line; I did not read those and do not report them as verified.
stance: commentator (Augustine, exegete). Reporting his argument; the claim about adoption is his, not a legal source.

orig_url: https://www.sefaria.org/api/texts/Genesis.48.5-6?context=0 (Hebrew read; version: JPS Tanakh Gender-Sensitive Edition, Hebrew = Masoretic text)
quote_en: are mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine.
licence_note: KJV English (Gutenberg #10) public domain. Hebrew: Masoretic text (public domain); the Sefaria record names the JPS Gender-Sensitive Edition, whose English translation is CC BY-NC (not quoted). Rashi Hebrew: public domain; Rashi English on Sefaria not quoted (licence not shown on the page).
from_: are mine; as Reuben and Simeon
what_it_shows: Jacob declares Ephraim and Manasseh, born to Joseph in Egypt, to be his own (the text says 'mine' and 'as Reuben and Simeon'), so that they stand as sons of Jacob like his other sons. Gen 48:6 then says Joseph's later children 'shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance'. Rashi on 48:5 explains that Ephraim and Manasseh are 'counted amongst my other sons, to receive a portion in the Land each for himself'.
context: Jacob, dying in Egypt, adopts Joseph's two sons born there before Jacob came (48:5). In the same speech he sets out what happens to later-born children (48:6). The Hebrew of Gen 41:45 and 41:50–52 (read on Sefaria) confirms that Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore Manasseh and Ephraim to Joseph, so these sons were begotten by Joseph and then taken into Jacob's line.
limits: (1) The verse does not use the word 'adopt'; it says 'shall be mine'. The adoption reading is an interpretive reading (Augustine, J-03; Rashi). (2) The verse does not mention land or tribe in 48:5; the land share is Rashi's reading (Rashi: 'to receive a portion in the Land'). (3) Rashi on 48:6 limits the case: later-born children of Joseph 'shall not be in the count of my sons, but shall be included within the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, and shall have no name among the tribes with respect to inheritance'. So the tribal name passes to Ephraim and Manasseh, not to every descendant. (4) Rashi on 48:6 also says that only these two bore the name 'tribe' when the land was divided by lot (Num 26:55 style reasoning). (5) The hint's wording ('shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are mine') is a paraphrase; the KJV reads 'are mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine.' (6) Gen 41:50–52 says the sons were born to Joseph, so they were begotten, not adopted, before being taken by Jacob; this is consistent with the text but shows that the adoption is a transfer of standing, not a claim of blood.
stance: reporting (Genesis read in Hebrew; Rashi read in Hebrew). Rashi's view is a commentator's view.

ref: Eusebius, Church History 3.19.1–3.20.2 (quoting Hegesippus); see also 3.12 and 3.32.3–4
orig_url: not read (Greek of Eusebius HE 3.19–20 not yet located)
quote_en: Information was given that they belonged to the family of David, and they were brought to the Emperor Domitian by the Evocatus.
licence_note: English: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, NPNF2 vol. 1 (1890), public domain. Page read at newadvent.org.
from_: Information was given that they belonged
to: brought to the Emperor Domitian by the Evocatus.
keys: belonged to the family of David
what_it_shows: The source (Eusebius quoting Hegesippus) reports that under Domitian, grandsons of Jude (said to be a brother of the Lord 'according to the flesh') were accused and brought to the emperor on the ground that they belonged to the family of David, and that they answered that they were descendants of David. It says nothing about how the Davidic descent was reckoned, and does not mention adoption.
context: Eusebius book 3 covers the period after the Jewish war. Ch. 12 reports (via Hegesippus) that Vespasian ordered all of David's lineage to be sought. Ch. 19–20 report that Domitian ordered the descendants of David to be slain, and that accusers (described as 'heretics') charged Jude's grandsons; Domitian questioned them, found them to be poor farmers, and let them go. Ch. 32 reports that Symeon son of Clopas was accused of being 'a descendant of David and a Christian' under Trajan, and that searches for David's family also arrested his accusers.
limits: (1) The passage is not about adoption or legal sonship; the source does not say how the grandsons were descended from David (through Joseph, through Mary, or otherwise). Using it for lineage by adoption would be an inference. (2) The accusers were described as 'heretics' in the report, and the claim of Davidic descent was made against Christians by hostile informers. (3) The text itself does not say the family was Davidic through Joseph; Eusebius records only that the family was said to be of David's lineage. (4) Eusebius writes that the grandsons 'said to have been a brother of the Saviour according to the flesh'; the 'brother' relation is also reported, not verified by the source. (5) Hegesippus is known only from Eusebius's quotation (the original is lost); I read Eusebius's text only. (6) Eusebius 3.19 also reports that the family were 'related to Christ himself'; no genealogy is given.
stance: reporting (Eusebius quoting Hegesippus; hostile and neutral witnesses in the account)

ref: Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 100 (read) and 43 (read in ch. 43 text); see also 88 and 120
orig_url: not read (Greek of Justin Dialogue not located)
quote_en: either because of His birth by the Virgin, who was, as I said, of the family of David and Jacob, and Isaac, and Abraham
licence_note: English: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe), public domain. Page read at newadvent.org.
from_: either because of His birth by the Virgin
to: of the family of David and Jacob, and Isaac, and Abraham
keys: of the family of David and Jacob
what_it_shows: Justin says Christ was born of a virgin 'of the family of David and Jacob, and Isaac, and Abraham' (ch. 100), and in ch. 43 of 'the family of Abraham and tribe of Judah, and of David'. In both places the Davidic descent is attached to the Virgin (Mary), not to Joseph, and no legal transfer is described.
context: Justin (c. mid-2nd century) argues with the Jew Trypho that the Christ's line comes from David through the Virgin. In ch. 88 (read) he says that Jesus 'was considered to be the son of Joseph the carpenter', a popular impression, and in ch. 78 Matthew's Joseph is named 'the spouse of Mary' in the Herod story. Justin's usage thus links the Davidic descent to the mother.
limits: (1) Justin does not mention Joseph's adoption or any legal sonship for Jesus; he attributes the Davidic descent to the Virgin (ch. 100, 120). This is the main contrary witness within the early Church: Davidic descent via Mary. (2) In ch. 88 he says 'He was considered to be the son of Joseph the carpenter', which is a popular view, not a legal claim by Justin. (3) Ch. 43 says 'born of a virgin, of the family of Abraham and tribe of Judah, and of David' with no mechanism given. (4) Justin's date is mid-2nd century (approx.; not on the page). (5) The Dialogue is a Christian apologetic text; the Jewish speaker Trypho is not a source for Davidic status.
stance: reporting (Justin's own arguments; his claims about Davidic descent are made through Mary)

ref: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 1.14 (questions) and 2.7–8 (answer)
quote_en: Hence it is evident that Joseph also was of the same. Yes, for there was a law, which bade that it should not be lawful to take a wife from any other stock, but from the same tribe.
licence_note: English: George Prevost, revised by M.B. Riddle, NPNF1 vol. 10 (1888), public domain. Page read at newadvent.org.
from_: Hence it is evident that Joseph also
keys: Hence it is evident that Joseph also
what_it_shows: Chrysostom argues from the Mosaic rule against marrying outside the tribe that Joseph was of David's house (Luke 1:27), so that Mary, betrothed to him, must also be of David's line. He explains that Matthew traces Joseph because women were not normally named in genealogies (Hom. 2.8). The passage concerns endogamy and reckoning through men; it does not describe adoption.
context: In Homily 1 (sec. 14) Chrysostom lists the questions the genealogy raises, beginning with 'wherefore the genealogy of Joseph is traced, who was not father of Christ'. In Homily 2 (sec. 7–8) he answers: the Virgin is of David's house, and Joseph likewise, because a righteous man 'would not have endured to take a wife from another race'; Joseph's genealogy is given because the law did not trace women's genealogies.
limits: (1) Chrysostom states in his own question that Joseph 'was not father of Christ' (Hom. 1, sec. 14). (2) He uses Joseph's genealogy as a way of showing Mary's Davidic descent, and in Hom. 2 he says 'the Virgin likewise is sprung from thence'. So the Davidic line is also presented through Mary. (3) He gives no legal theory of adoption, levirate or naming; the link is Joseph's endogamous marriage. (4) The argument depends on the Mosaic endogamy rule, which he applies to a marriage in the Gospel; he says this rule forbade marrying from 'another lineage', so Joseph's descent and Mary's come together. (5) Homilies in the 4th century (c. 390 AD; not on the page) are a late witness, not an early legal source.

ref: Jerome, Adversus Helvidium (The Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary) §4 (on Matt 1:18–25 and the name 'father')
quote_en: First, that by the genealogy of Joseph, whose kinswoman Mary was, Mary's origin might also be shown.
licence_note: English: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF2 vol. 6 (1893), public domain. Page read at newadvent.org.
from_: by the genealogy of Joseph, whose kinswoman
to: Mary's origin might also be shown.
keys: Mary's origin might also be shown
what_it_shows: Jerome says that Joseph's genealogy is given to show Mary's origin, because Mary was Joseph's kinswoman. In the same section he says the evangelists call Joseph 'father' according to the prevailing opinion, and states that Joseph was not really the father of the Saviour; the name was used 'to preserve the reputation of Mary'.
context: Against the Christian Helvidius, who argued that Mary had other children, Jerome (c. 383 AD; date from general knowledge, not on the page) argues for Mary's perpetual virginity and that Joseph's marriage to her was in name. In section 4 he explains the reasons why Scripture says Joseph was Mary's husband only in name (three reasons are given), the reason for Joseph's genealogy, and why Joseph is called 'father' of the Lord.
limits: (1) Jerome states explicitly: 'Not (as I said before) that Joseph was really the father of the Saviour: but that, to preserve the reputation of Mary, he had thoughts of putting her away privily'. This is a direct denial that Joseph was the real father, and it gives the 'father' usage a conventional reason. (2) Jerome does not use the word 'adopt' in this work (text searched). (3) He ties Mary's origin to Joseph's line through kinship ('kinswoman'), not through adoption or law. (4) Jerome's opening summary states that Joseph 'was only putatively, not really, the husband of Mary' (line of the summary of arguments). (5) This is a polemical treatise, and section 4 is about the evangelists' usage, so it is a commentator's reading, not a statement of Jewish law.
stance: commentator (Jerome, polemical; quoting the evangelists' 'father' usage as he reads it)

ref: Ignatius, To the Ephesians 18:2 (read in ANF); see also Eph 20:2 in same text
orig_url: not read (Greek of Eph 18:2 not located)
quote_en: For our God, Jesus Christ, was, according to the appointment of God, conceived in the womb by Mary, of the seed of David, but by the Holy Ghost.
licence_note: English: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1 (1885), public domain. Page read at newadvent.org (fathers/0104.htm).
from_: For our God, Jesus Christ, was, according
keys: conceived in the womb by Mary
what_it_shows: Ignatius says that Jesus, 'our God', was conceived in the womb by Mary, 'of the seed of David', and by the Holy Spirit. The Davidic 'seed' is linked to Mary, and Joseph is not mentioned in this sentence. In Eph 20:2 (same ANF text) he writes 'Jesus Christ, who was of the seed of David according to the flesh, being both the Son of man and the Son of God', again without naming Joseph.
context: Ignatius (early 2nd century; date from general knowledge, not on the page) writes in a list of hidden mysteries in ch. 18–19 (ch. 19 follows).
limits: (1) This is a witness that gives the Davidic 'seed' with Mary as the agent of conception and no mention of Joseph; it counts against a Joseph-based (adoptive) line as the only route. (2) The text does not say that Mary's line is the only route of descent, and does not say that Joseph's adoption is absent. (3) 'According to the flesh' (Eph 20:2) is a statement about the flesh, not about law. (4) Eph 18:2 is a short doctrinal list, not an argument about genealogy. (5) The Greek of Eph 18:2 was not read (no quote_orig).

context: Smyrnaeans is an early 2nd-century letter of Ignatius (date from general knowledge, not on the page), written from custody on the way to Rome, against docetic teaching. The phrase is in the opening section, followed by 'Son of God by the will and power of God'.

ref: Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.21.9 (and III.21.8 on Joseph's paternity); III.9.1 for the Davidic 'virgin' line
orig_url: not read (Greek/Latin of AH III.21 not located; Armenian and Latin fragments exist, not checked)
quote_en: But besides, if indeed He had been the son of Joseph, He could not, according to Jeremiah, be either king or heir. For Joseph is shown to be the son of Joachim and Jechoniah, as also Matthew sets forth in his pedigree.
licence_note: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1 (1885), public domain. Page read at newadvent.org.
from_: But besides, if indeed He had been
to: as also Matthew sets forth in his pedigree.
keys: could not, according to Jeremiah, be either king or heir
Joseph is shown to be the son of Joachim and Jechoniah
what_it_shows: Irenaeus argues that if Jesus had been the son of Joseph, he could not be king or heir of David, because (by Jer 22:24–30) Jechoniah's posterity were disinherited from the kingdom, and Matthew's pedigree traces Joseph through Jechoniah. He concludes that Christ was born of the Virgin, 'of the virgin of [the house of] David' (III.9.1), so his kingship comes through the mother's side.
context: Irenaeus (late 2nd century; date from general knowledge, not on the page) argues in Book III against those who said Christ was begotten of Joseph (the opponents are not named in the section read). Section 8 says that if Jesus were 'the son of Joseph', he could not be 'greater than David'. Section 9 gives the Jeremiah argument.
limits: (1) This is a direct statement against the claim that Joseph's line (through Jechoniah) gives kingship or inheritance to Jesus. It counts against the thesis that the legal line through Joseph transmits royal status, although Irenaeus is writing about the natural son of Joseph, not an adopted one. He does not discuss adoption, levirate or legal fiction at this point. (2) The passage relies on Jer 22:24–30 (the curse on Jechoniah) as he reads it. (3) Irenaeus's argument makes the Davidic line run through the Virgin (III.9.1, 'of the virgin of [the house of] David'; and in III.21, 'the Virgin, herself of the lineage of David', section not checked), so he counts Mary's line as the route. (4) The word 'adoption' appears in III.21 only in the sense of Gal 4:4–5 (the adoption of humanity into God's sons), not for Joseph. (5) Irenaeus is a Christian polemical witness, not a legal source; he does not say what Jewish law did in adoption cases.
stance: commentator (Irenaeus, polemic against those who said Christ was Joseph's son); the argument is his, the Jeremiah text is quoted by him

what_it_shows: Luke says that Joseph himself was 'of the house and lineage of David' (2:4) and that Mary was betrothed to 'a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David' (1:27). The text places Joseph in David's line but does not say how, and does not say that Jesus takes Joseph's line by adoption or law.
